subject: maths
title: Multiplication
seo_title: Year 5 Multiplication Worksheets: Free Maths with Answer Key (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Solve problems involving multiplication of larger numbers by one- or two-digit numbers, choosing efficient calculation strategies and using digital tools where appropriate; check the reasonableness of answers
meta_desc: Free Year 5 maths worksheets on multiplication, aligned to the Australian Curriculum (AC9M5N06): mental strategies, the area model, short multiplication, long multiplication with a place-holder zero, estimating to check, and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key, great for NAPLAN practice.
key_big: Multiply one digit at a time. For a 2-digit number, make two rows and start row 2 with a place-holder zero.
key_sub: 38 × 24 = 38 × 4 + 38 × 20 = 152 + 760 = 912. Then estimate to check: 40 × 20 = 800, so 912 is reasonable.
body_html:
Mental strategies: use facts you know

Many big multiplications are a multiplication fact in disguise. 60 is 6 tens, so 60 × 7 is 6 × 7 = 42 tens = 420.

Other quick strategies: change the order (25 × 7 × 4 = 25 × 4 × 7 = 100 × 7 = 700), double and halve (16 × 25 = 8 × 50 = 400), × 5 is × 10, then halve (46 × 5 = 460 ÷ 2 = 230) and use a near number (99 × 6 = 600 − 6 = 594).

The area model: partition by place value

Split each number into tens and ones. Draw a rectangle with one part for each pair. Multiply each part, then add all the parts.

Short multiplication: up to 4 digits × 1 digit

Line up the ones. Start with the ones column. When a product is 10 or more, write the ones digit and regroup the tens into the next column as a small digit. Multiply first, then add the regrouped digit.

Long multiplication: × a 2-digit number

Make one row for each digit. Row 1 multiplies by the ones digit. Row 2 multiplies by the tens digit, so it starts with a place-holder zero (green). Then add the two rows.

3-digit × 2-digit

243 × 36 = ?

Row 1: 243 × 6 = 1458. Row 2: write 0, then 243 × 3 = 729, so 7290. Add: 1458 + 7290 = 8748.

Answer: 8748

Check that your answer is reasonable

Round each number, then multiply. 243 × 36 is about 200 × 40 = 8000, so 8748 makes sense. An answer like 2187 (no place-holder zero) is far too small.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Losing or adding a zero (60 × 7 = 42 or 4200)60 is 6 tens: 6 × 7 = 42 tens = 420
No place-holder zero (38 × 24 = 152 + 76 = 228)Row 2 is × 20, so write 0 first: 760
Not adding a regrouped digit (38 × 4 = 122)Write it small and add it: 3 × 4 + 3 = 15, so 152
Adding the regrouped digit firstMultiply first, then add: 3 × 4 + 3 = 15, not (3 + 3) × 4
Only two parts in the area model (34 × 26 = 600 + 24)There are four parts: 600 + 80 + 180 + 24 = 884
Estimating with the wrong rounding (386 → 300)386 is closer to 400: 400 × 40 = 16 000

faq.q: What multiplication do Year 5 students learn in Australia?
faq.a: Under the Australian Curriculum (AC9M5N06) they multiply larger numbers by one- or two-digit numbers, choose efficient strategies such as the area model or long multiplication, and check that answers are reasonable by estimating.

faq.q: How do you teach long multiplication in Year 5?
faq.a: Start with 2-digit × 2-digit. Multiply by the ones digit for row 1, write a place-holder zero and multiply by the tens digit for row 2, then add the rows: 38 × 24 = 152 + 760 = 912.

faq.q: What is the area model for multiplication?
faq.a: It partitions both numbers by place value and draws a rectangle with a part for each pair. For 34 × 26 the parts are 600, 80, 180 and 24, which add to 884.

faq.q: Is multiplication on the Year 5 NAPLAN numeracy test?
faq.a: Yes. NAPLAN numeracy is based on the Australian Curriculum, so Year 5 students meet multiplication questions and word problems. Practising written methods and estimating helps them work accurately.

items.q: Double, then double again, to find 37 × 4.
items.e: × 4 is double, then double again. Double 37 = 74. Double 74 = 148. Doubling only once gives 74; three times gives 296.

items.q: What is 30 × 400?
items.e: Use 3 × 4 = 12. 30 has one zero and 400 has two zeros, so put back three zeros: 30 × 400 = 12 000.

items.q: What is 2 × 36 × 5?
items.e: You can multiply in any order. Change the order: 2 × 5 = 10, then 10 × 36 = 360. Multiply all three numbers, not just two.
24 is double 12, so 24 × 7 is double 84 = 168.

items.q: What is 16 × 25? (Hint: halve one number and double the other.)
items.e: Halve 16 and double 25: 16 × 25 = 8 × 50 = 4 × 100 = 400. If you double one number, you must halve the other.

items.q: What is 5 × 17 × 2?
items.e: You can multiply in any order. Change the order: 5 × 2 = 10, then 10 × 17 = 170. Multiply all three numbers, not just two.

items.q: What is 60 × 7?
items.e: 60 is 6 tens. 6 × 7 = 42, so 6 tens × 7 = 42 tens = 420.

items.q: What is 3000 × 7?
items.e: 3000 is 3 thousands. 3 × 7 = 21, so 3 thousands × 7 = 21 thousands = 21 000.

items.q: What is 58 × 100?
items.e: × 100 makes every digit 100 times bigger: the 8 ones become 8 hundreds. 58 × 100 = 5800 (two zeros on the end).

items.q: What is 400 × 6?
items.e: 400 is 4 hundreds. 4 × 6 = 24, so 4 hundreds × 6 = 24 hundreds = 2400.

items.q: What is 99 × 6? (Hint: 99 is 1 less than 100.)
What is 27 × 1000?
items.e: × 1000 moves every digit three places to the left: 27 × 1000 = 27 000 (three zeros on the end).

items.q: What is 50 × 8?
items.e: 50 is 5 tens. 5 × 8 = 40, so 5 tens × 8 = 40 tens = 400. The 0 in 40 is part of the fact, so do not drop it.

items.q: What is 900 × 8?
items.e: 900 is 9 hundreds. 9 × 8 = 72, so 9 hundreds × 8 = 72 hundreds = 7200.

items.q: What is 25 × 4 × 7?
items.e: You can multiply in any order. 25 × 4 = 100, then 100 × 7 = 700. Multiply all three numbers, not just two.

items.q: What is 18 × 50?
items.e: × 50 is the same as × 100, then halve. 18 × 100 = 1800. Half of 1800 = 900.
24 is one less than 25, so take away one 8: 200 − 8 = 192.

items.q: What is 19 × 8?
What is 70 × 80?
items.e: Use 7 × 8 = 56. 70 has one zero and 80 has one zero, so put back two zeros: 70 × 80 = 5600.

items.q: Multiply by 10, then halve, to find 46 × 5.
items.e: × 5 is the same as × 10, then halve. 46 × 10 = 460. Half of 460 = 230.

items.q: Which parts add up to 16 × 26?
items.e: Each part of one number multiplies each part of the other, so there are 4 parts. Partition 16 = 10 + 6 and 26 = 20 + 6. 10 × 20 = 200, 6 × 20 = 120, 10 × 6 = 60, 6 × 6 = 36. Add: 200 + 120 + 60 + 36 = 416.

items.q: Which is equal to 79 × 5?
items.e: Partition 79 into 70 + 9. Both parts must be multiplied by 5: 70 × 5 + 9 × 5 = 350 + 45 = 395.

items.e: Each part of one number multiplies each part of the other, so there are 4 parts. Partition 53 = 50 + 3 and 58 = 50 + 8. 50 × 50 = 2500, 3 × 50 = 150, 50 × 8 = 400, 3 × 8 = 24. Add: 2500 + 150 + 400 + 24 = 3074.

items.q: Which is equal to 45 × 7?
items.e: Partition 45 into 40 + 5. Both parts must be multiplied by 7: 40 × 7 + 5 × 7 = 280 + 35 = 315.

sets.title: Long multiplication and checking by estimating

items.q: What number goes in the dashed box?
items.e: Add the two rows with column addition, and add every regrouped digit: 4640 + 27 840 = 32 480.

items.q: Use long multiplication.
Sienna got 45 × 49 = 2165. What mistake did she make?
c: Did not add a regrouped digit
items.e: Row 1 should be 405, not 365: 5 × 9 = 45, write 5, regroup 4; 4 × 9 + 4 = 40, write 40. The regrouped digits were not added. The correct answer is 2205.

items.q: What number goes in the dashed box?
items.e: Row 2 multiplies by the tens digit, so it is 47 × 50. Write the place-holder 0 first, then 47 × 5: 7 × 5 = 35, write 5, regroup 3; 4 × 5 + 3 = 23, write 23. The row is 2350, not 235. Check: 329 + 2350 = 2679.

Calculate 14 × 73.
items.e: Row 1: 14 × 3 = 42. Row 2: 14 × 70 = 980 (write the place-holder 0, then 14 × 7 = 98). Add: 42 + 980 = 1022.

Which is the best estimate for 67 × 48?
items.e: Round 67 to the nearest ten: 70 (the next digit is 7, so round up). Round 48 to the nearest ten: 50 (round up). 70 × 50 = 3500. The exact answer is 3216, close to 3500.

Ava got 42 × 59 = 588. What mistake did she make?
c: Did not add a regrouped digit
items.e: Row 2 should be 42 × 50 = 2100, but she wrote 210. The place-holder 0 is missing. The correct answer is 2478.

items.q: Amelia works out 712 × 29 = 20 648. Estimate to check. Is her answer reasonable?
items.e: Estimate: 712 × 29 is about 700 × 30 = 21 000. 20 648 is close to 21 000, so the answer is reasonable.

items.q: Calculate 36 × 23.
items.e: Row 1: 36 × 3 = 108. Row 2: 36 × 20 = 720 (write the place-holder 0, then 36 × 2 = 72). Add: 108 + 720 = 828.

items.q: Cooper works out 286 × 34 = 2002. Estimate to check. Is his answer reasonable?
items.e: Estimate: 286 × 34 is about 300 × 30 = 9000. 2002 is far from 9000, so it cannot be right. Cooper forgot the place-holder 0 in row 2. The correct answer is 9724.

items.q: Which is the best estimate for 386 × 42?
items.e: Round 386 to the nearest hundred: 400 (the next digit is 8, so round up). Round 42 to the nearest ten: 40 (round down). 400 × 40 = 16 000. The exact answer is 16 212, close to 16 000.

sets.title: Word problems: seats, excursions, money and distance

items.q: At swimming training, Leo swims 36 laps of a 50 m pool. How far does he swim?
items.e: Equal groups: 36 laps × 50 m, so multiply 50 × 36. Row 1: 50 × 6 = 300. Row 2: 50 × 30 = 1500 (write the place-holder 0, then 50 × 3 = 150). Add: 300 + 1500 = 1800.

items.q: A stand at the cricket ground has 24 rows of 45 seats. 958 people are sitting in the stand. How many seats are empty?
A bakery makes 1365 sausage rolls every day. How many sausage rolls does it make in 6 days?
items.e: Equal groups: 6 days × 1365 sausage rolls, so multiply 1365 × 6. Ones: 5 × 6 = 30. Write 0, regroup 3. Tens: 6 × 6 + 3 = 39. Write 9, regroup 3. Hundreds: 3 × 6 + 3 = 21. Write 1, regroup 2. Thousands: 1 × 6 + 2 = 8. Write 8. Answer: 8190.

items.q: Each school bus seats 57 students. How many students can 14 buses carry?
items.e: Equal groups: 14 buses × 57 students, so multiply 57 × 14. Row 1: 57 × 4 = 228. Row 2: 57 × 10 = 570 (write the place-holder 0, then 57 × 1 = 57). Add: 228 + 570 = 798.

items.q: A school excursion to the zoo costs $35 for each student. 28 students in Year 5 are going. What is the total cost?
items.e: Equal groups: 28 students × $35, so multiply 35 × 28. Row 1: 35 × 8 = 280. Row 2: 35 × 20 = 700 (write the place-holder 0, then 35 × 2 = 70). Add: 280 + 700 = 980.

items.q: A Year 5 excursion costs $14 a student for entry and $9 a student for the bus. 28 students go. What is the total cost?
Tickets to a show cost $42 each. The best estimate of the cost of 19 tickets is …
items.e: Round 19 to 20 and $42 to $40. 20 × $40 = $800. The exact cost is 19 × $42 = $798, very close. (Rounding 42 up to 50 gives $1000, which is too far off.)

items.q: The school canteen sells 136 meat pies each week. How many pies does it sell in 9 weeks?
items.e: Equal groups: 9 weeks × 136 pies, so multiply 136 × 9. Ones: 6 × 9 = 54. Write 4, regroup 5. Tens: 3 × 9 + 5 = 32. Write 2, regroup 3. Hundreds: 1 × 9 + 3 = 12. Write 12. Answer: 1224.

items.q: A netball club buys 9 new netballs at $47 each. How much does it spend?
items.e: Equal groups: 9 netballs × $47, so multiply 47 × 9. Ones: 7 × 9 = 63. Write 3, regroup 6. Tens: 4 × 9 + 6 = 42. Write 42. Answer: 423.

items.q: For the athletics carnival, the school orders 35 boxes of water bottles. Each box holds 24 bottles. How many bottles is that?
items.e: Equal groups: 35 boxes × 24 bottles, so multiply 24 × 35. Row 1: 24 × 5 = 120. Row 2: 24 × 30 = 720 (write the place-holder 0, then 24 × 3 = 72). Add: 120 + 720 = 840.

items.q: A mango farm in Queensland packs 1235 trays in a week. Each tray holds 18 mangoes. How many mangoes is that?
items.e: Equal groups: 1235 trays × 18 mangoes, so multiply 1235 × 18. Row 1: 1235 × 8 = 9880. Row 2: 1235 × 10 = 12 350 (write the place-holder 0, then 1235 × 1 = 1235). Add: 9880 + 12 350 = 22 230.

items.q: A section of a footy stadium has 48 rows with 36 seats in each row. How many seats are in the section?
items.e: Equal groups: 48 rows × 36 seats, so multiply 36 × 48. Row 1: 36 × 8 = 288. Row 2: 36 × 40 = 1440 (write the place-holder 0, then 36 × 4 = 144). Add: 288 + 1440 = 1728.

items.q: The town's footy ground holds 6250 people. The city stadium holds 8 times as many. How many people does the stadium hold?
items.e: 8 times as many means multiply: 6250 × 8. Think 6000 × 8 = 48 000 and 250 × 8 = 2000. 48 000 + 2000 = 50 000 people.

items.q: A cricket club buys 24 new cricket balls at $18 each. How much does it spend?
items.e: Equal groups: 24 balls × $18, so multiply 18 × 24. Row 1: 18 × 4 = 72. Row 2: 18 × 20 = 360 (write the place-holder 0, then 18 × 2 = 36). Add: 72 + 360 = 432.

items.q: A school buys 27 tablets at $312 each. Chloe says the total is $2808. Is her answer reasonable?
items.e: Estimate: $312 is about $300 and 27 is about 30. 30 × $300 = $9000. $2808 is far too small. Chloe forgot the place-holder 0 in row 2. The correct total is 27 × $312 = $8424.

items.q: A box holds 144 pencils. The school office orders 23 boxes. How many pencils is that?
items.e: Equal groups: 23 boxes × 144 pencils, so multiply 144 × 23. Row 1: 144 × 3 = 432. Row 2: 144 × 20 = 2880 (write the place-holder 0, then 144 × 2 = 288). Add: 432 + 2880 = 3312.

items.q: The school hall is set up with 32 rows of chairs. Each row has 26 chairs. How many chairs are there?
items.e: Equal groups: 32 rows × 26 chairs, so multiply 26 × 32. Row 1: 26 × 2 = 52. Row 2: 26 × 30 = 780 (write the place-holder 0, then 26 × 3 = 78). Add: 52 + 780 = 832.

items.q: Ruby's family drives 245 km every week to visit her grandparents' farm. How far do they drive in 12 weeks?
items.e: Equal groups: 12 weeks × 245 km, so multiply 245 × 12. Row 1: 245 × 2 = 490. Row 2: 245 × 10 = 2450 (write the place-holder 0, then 245 × 1 = 245). Add: 490 + 2450 = 2940.

items.q: A delivery truck drives 386 km every week. How far does it drive in 7 weeks?
items.e: Equal groups: 7 weeks × 386 km, so multiply 386 × 7. Ones: 6 × 7 = 42. Write 2, regroup 4. Tens: 8 × 7 + 4 = 60. Write 0, regroup 6. Hundreds: 3 × 7 + 6 = 27. Write 27. Answer: 2702.

items.q: The school library orders 165 new books at $14 each. What is the total cost?
items.e: Equal groups: 165 books × $14, so multiply 165 × 14. Row 1: 165 × 4 = 660. Row 2: 165 × 10 = 1650 (write the place-holder 0, then 165 × 1 = 165). Add: 660 + 1650 = 2310.
